blocks.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with recurrent postcoital bleeding and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Take a focused gynaecological history and discuss your differential diagnoses.
A 48-year-old woman presents with persistent vaginal bleeding. Perform a speculum examination and report your findings.
You are shown an image of an irregular, friable cervical mass that bleeds on contact. Describe the findings and state the most likely diagnosis.
A cervical biopsy has confirmed invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Explain the diagnosis and the next steps to the patient.
A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with early-stage cervical cancer. Discuss staging investigations and treatment options.
Cervical cancer is a malignant tumour arising from the cervix, the lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina.
The majority of cases are associated with persistent infection by high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV).
Arises from the squamous epithelium, commonly around the transformation zone of the cervix.
Arises from glandular cells of the endocervical canal. It may be less readily visible on routine speculum examination if located higher in the canal.
Include tumours with both glandular and squamous differentiation, as well as uncommon neuroendocrine and other malignant tumours.

content_groups.group_title: Important anatomical concept: the transformation zone

blocks.text: The transformation zone is the region where the original columnar epithelium is replaced by squamous metaplastic epithelium. Most cervical precancers and many invasive cancers arise in this region.
Persistent high-risk HPV infection, especially HPV 16 and 18.
Early onset of sexual activity and multiple sexual partners, which may increase HPV exposure.
Smoking.
HIV infection or other causes of immunosuppression.
Lack of access to cervical screening and follow-up.
Previous high-grade cervical intraepithelial lesions.
Inadequate HPV vaccination coverage.
Important: HPV infection is common and does not mean a person has cancer. Most infections clear spontaneously; persistent infection with oncogenic HPV types is the major concern.

items: Viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 interfere with tumour-suppressor pathways
Progression in a subset of cases to invasive cervical cancer

blocks.text: HPV E6 promotes degradation of p53, while E7 disrupts the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumour-suppressor pathway. These changes can permit uncontrolled cell proliferation.
Progression is not inevitable. Screening and treatment of precancerous lesions can prevent many cases of invasive cancer.
Cervical cancer may be asymptomatic and detected through screening or investigation of abnormal bleeding.
Possible symptoms include:
Postcoital bleeding.
Intermenstrual bleeding.
Unusually heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding.
Postmenopausal bleeding.
Persistent watery or blood-stained vaginal discharge.
Persistent pelvic or lower abdominal pain.
Foul-smelling vaginal discharge.
Dyspareunia.
Back pain.
Unilateral or bilateral leg swelling.
Haematuria or rectal bleeding.
Urinary obstruction or hydronephrosis.
Weight loss, fatigue and anaemia.
Vesicovaginal or rectovaginal fistula in advanced cases.

OSCE red flag: Postcoital bleeding, particularly when recurrent or associated with a suspicious cervix, requires prompt investigation. It should not automatically be attributed to infection, contraception or cervical ectropion.

Introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity.
Explain the purpose of the consultation.
Obtain consent.
Ensure privacy and offer a chaperone if an intimate examination may be needed.
Use non-judgmental language when discussing sexual history.
Example:

"I understand you have been experiencing vaginal bleeding. I'd like to ask some questions about the bleeding, your menstrual and reproductive history, and any other symptoms so that we can understand what may be causing it."
Use a structured approach.
When did it begin?
Is it after intercourse, between periods or after menopause?
How much blood is lost?
Is it recurrent or persistent?
Is there associated pain?
Does it occur after vaginal examination or spontaneously?
Is it watery, blood-stained or offensive?
How long has it been present?
Is there associated itching, fever or pelvic pain?
Site, onset, duration and severity.
Relationship to intercourse or menstruation.
Radiation to the back or legs.
Urinary or bowel symptoms.
Ask about:
Age at menarche and menstrual pattern.
Last menstrual period and menopausal status.
Previous cervical screening results.
Previous HPV tests, colposcopy, cervical biopsies or treatment for precancer.
History of sexually transmitted infections.
Contraceptive use.
Previous pelvic inflammatory disease, where relevant.
Gravidity and parity.
Previous pregnancies and delivery history.
Current pregnancy possibility.
Sexual history, asked sensitively and only to the extent relevant to assessment.
HPV vaccination history.
HIV status or other immunosuppression, where appropriate.
Smoking history.
Current medications, including anticoagulants.
Previous pelvic radiotherapy or surgery.
Family support, emotional concerns and barriers to attending follow-up.

content_groups.group_title: F. Red flags requiring urgent assessment

blocks.text: Heavy ongoing bleeding with haemodynamic compromise.
Severe pelvic pain or suspected sepsis.
Acute kidney injury or urinary obstruction.
Significant haematuria or bowel obstruction.
Suspected advanced malignancy with rapidly worsening symptoms.

subsections.subsection_title: Examination of a patient with suspected cervical cancer

blocks.text: Assess:
General appearance and performance status.
Pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate.
Pallor.
Weight loss or cachexia.
Peripheral lymph nodes, including supraclavicular and inguinal nodes where indicated.
Lower limb oedema.
Hydration and general nutritional status.
Look for:
Abdominal distension.
Palpable pelvic or abdominal masses.
Suprapubic fullness suggesting bladder distension.
Ascites.
Hepatomegaly or other findings suggesting metastatic disease.
Renal angle tenderness.
Obtain consent, ensure adequate lighting and use a chaperone. Explain that the examination may cause some discomfort or bleeding.
Inspect the cervix for:
An irregular, ulcerated or exophytic mass.
A friable lesion that bleeds on contact.
Abnormal discharge.
Distortion or enlargement of the cervix.
A lesion extending into the vaginal fornices or vaginal walls.
An abnormal cervix that is difficult to visualise completely.
A small invasive lesion may not appear grossly obvious, and a normal-looking cervix does not exclude disease.
When appropriate and performed by a trained clinician, assess:
Cervical consistency and mobility.
Cervical or pelvic tenderness.
Uterine size and mobility.
Adnexal masses.
Possible parametrial thickening or fixation.
A specialist may use this examination to assess the parametrium and pelvic sidewalls when clinically indicated. It is not a substitute for histological diagnosis or imaging.
Critical OSCE point: A suspicious cervical lesion requires biopsy. Do not perform a routine cervical smear as a substitute for diagnostic assessment of a visible suspicious mass.

rows: Everted columnar epithelium; may cause contact bleeding
Smooth, often pedunculated lesion protruding from the cervical canal
Inflammation, discharge and contact bleeding; may be infective
Precancerous epithelial abnormality without stromal invasion
Particularly important in postmenopausal bleeding; may coexist with cervical disease
Vaginal lesion or bleeding, with the cervix potentially normal
Focal benign lesion that may cause abnormal bleeding
Pregnancy must be considered in reproductive-age patients
Bleeding related to intercourse, injury or examination

blocks.text: Do not reassure a patient solely because the cervix appears inflamed or because an infection is detected. Persistent or unexplained bleeding still requires appropriate assessment.
The aims are to confirm the diagnosis, determine histological subtype, establish the stage, assess fitness for treatment and identify complications.
A histopathological diagnosis is generally required before definitive cancer treatment. A biopsy may be taken during colposcopy or directly from a suspicious lesion.
Magnified examination of the cervix to identify abnormal epithelium and guide biopsy. It is particularly useful for assessing cervical precancers and selected lesions.
These are screening or triage tools, depending on the programme. They do not replace biopsy when invasive cancer is suspected.
Helps assess tumour size, stromal involvement, parametrial extension and adjacent pelvic structures.
Used when indicated to assess lymph nodes, distant disease or other staging questions. Availability and the preferred modality vary.
Ultrasound or other appropriate imaging may be needed if ureteric obstruction or hydronephrosis is suspected.
Full blood count.
Renal function and electrolytes.
Liver function tests when indicated.
HIV testing according to local guidance and with appropriate consent.
Pregnancy test where relevant.
Additional tests based on symptoms, stage and planned treatment.
Cystoscopy or proctoscopy may be considered for selected clinical indications, but they are not mandatory in every patient.
The FIGO system classifies cervical cancer according to the extent of disease. Imaging and pathology, where available and appropriate, supplement clinical assessment.

rows: Extends beyond the uterus but not to the pelvic wall or lower third of the vagina
Involves the lower third of the vagina, pelvic wall, causes hydronephrosis/non-functioning kidney, or involves qualifying pelvic/para-aortic lymph nodes
Extends beyond the true pelvis or involves the bladder or rectal mucosa, or has distant spread

blocks.text: IA: Microscopic invasive disease, with invasion measured in millimetres.
IB: Invasive disease confined to the cervix beyond stage IA.
IIA: Upper vaginal involvement without parametrial involvement.
IIB: Parametrial involvement, but not up to the pelvic wall.
IIIA: Lower third of the vagina involved, without pelvic wall extension.
IIIB: Pelvic wall extension and/or tumour-related hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney.
IIIC: Pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph node involvement, with subdivisions based on nodal location and imaging/pathological evidence.
IVA: Invasion of adjacent pelvic organs, such as bladder or rectal mucosa.
IVB: Distant metastases.
The detailed FIGO classification contains further subdivisions and measurement criteria. In an exam, learn the stage definitions from the version used by your training programme.
Treatment depends on stage, histology, tumour size, lymph node involvement, fertility wishes, comorbidities and available specialist services.
Management should be discussed by a multidisciplinary team, including gynaecological oncology, radiology, pathology, radiation oncology and medical oncology as appropriate.
CIN is not invasive cancer.
Management may include:
Surveillance for selected low-grade lesions.
Colposcopy-guided assessment.
Excisional treatment, such as LLETZ/LEEP, for appropriate high-grade lesions.
Ablative treatment for selected eligible lesions when invasive disease has been excluded.
Options for carefully selected patients may include:
Excisional procedures or conisation for certain microinvasive cancers.
Surgery, including selected fertility-sparing procedures.
Radical surgery with appropriate nodal assessment in eligible patients.
Fertility-sparing management requires careful selection and specialist counselling.

Concurrent chemoradiotherapy is a major treatment approach for many locally advanced cancers. This commonly combines external-beam radiotherapy, concurrent cisplatin when appropriate and brachytherapy.
The exact regimen depends on the patient's condition, renal function, stage and local protocols.
Options may include:
Systemic chemotherapy.
Immunotherapy in eligible patients, depending on tumour biomarkers and current indications.
Targeted treatment in selected cases.
Radiotherapy for symptom control or selected disease sites.
Palliative and supportive care.
Treat anaemia and bleeding.
Investigate and relieve urinary obstruction when present.
Manage pain, infection and malnutrition.
Offer psychological and social support.
Discuss fertility and sexual health where relevant.
Provide palliative care early when symptoms or advanced disease warrant it.
Important: Do not recommend a single treatment solely on the basis of a patient's age. Histology, stage, fertility goals, comorbidities and specialist assessment all matter.

subsections.subsection_title: Counselling a patient with a confirmed diagnosis

blocks.text: This is a common communication station.
A useful structure is SPIKES:
S — Set up a private, supportive environment.
P — Assess the patient's perception of the problem.
I — Ask how much information she wishes to receive.
K — Give knowledge in clear, manageable portions.
E — Respond empathetically to emotions.
S — Summarise the plan and agree on next steps.

"I have received the result of your biopsy, and it shows cancer of the cervix. I appreciate that this may be difficult news to hear. I want to reassure you that we will not leave you to face this alone.

The next step is to determine the extent of the disease and review the results with the specialist team. Treatment depends on the stage and the specific type of cancer. For some women, surgery is appropriate; for others, radiotherapy with chemotherapy is the preferred treatment.
I would like to explain each step, answer your questions and discuss any concerns you have, including fertility, relationships and the practical arrangements for treatment."
Allow silence and time for questions. Avoid promising a cure before staging or giving a prognosis without sufficient information.
Q1. What is the most important risk factor for cervical cancer?
Persistent infection with high-risk HPV, particularly types 16 and 18.
Q2. What is the most common histological type?
Squamous cell carcinoma.
Q3. What are the classical symptoms?
Postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, postmenopausal bleeding and persistent abnormal vaginal discharge.
Q4. What is the difference between CIN and invasive cervical cancer?
CIN is a precancerous epithelial lesion without invasion through the basement membrane. Invasive cancer has penetrated the basement membrane into cervical stroma.
Q5. What is the transformation zone?
The region where the squamous and columnar epithelial junction changes, including areas of squamous metaplasia. It is the principal site where many cervical precancers develop.
Q6. How is cervical cancer confirmed?
Histopathological examination of an appropriate biopsy, interpreted in the clinical context.
Q7. Can a normal cervical smear exclude cervical cancer in a patient with a suspicious lesion?
No. A screening test does not replace diagnostic assessment of a suspicious lesion. Prompt specialist assessment and biopsy are required.
Q8. What is the role of HPV vaccination?

It prevents infection with important oncogenic HPV types and reduces the risk of cervical precancers and cancers. It does not treat an established cancer and does not eliminate the need for screening.
Q9. What is the standard treatment approach for many locally advanced cervical cancers?
Concurrent chemoradiotherapy, usually incorporating external-beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy, with concurrent chemotherapy when appropriate.
Q10. Which structures may be affected in advanced cervical cancer?
The parametrium, vagina, pelvic sidewall, ureters, bladder, rectum, pelvic and para-aortic lymph nodes, and distant organs.
Failing to ask about postcoital and postmenopausal bleeding.
Attributing all bleeding to cervicitis or contraception.
Confusing CIN with invasive cancer.
Ordering cytology alone for a visibly suspicious cervical mass.
Forgetting biopsy and histopathology.
Giving definitive treatment advice without staging.
Ignoring renal function and possible ureteric obstruction.
Failing to discuss HPV vaccination and prevention.
Communicating the diagnosis insensitively or giving false reassurance.
Neglecting fertility, sexual health, psychosocial support and follow-up.
B — Bleeding after intercourse.
L — Lower abdominal or pelvic pain.
O — Offensive or watery discharge.
O — Ongoing intermenstrual or postmenopausal bleeding.
D — Distant disease symptoms, such as leg oedema or weight loss.
B — Biopsy for histological confirmation.
I — Imaging for staging.
O — Organ function: renal function, blood count and other relevant tests.
P — Pelvic assessment, including examination and colposcopy as appropriate.
S — Screening history and HPV-related results.
Y — Your multidisciplinary treatment plan.
Pre-invasive: surveillance or treatment of precancer as indicated.
Early invasive: selected surgery or fertility-sparing treatment.
Locally advanced: usually chemoradiotherapy.
Metastatic/recurrent: individualised systemic treatment, radiotherapy and supportive care.

Treat empirically for cervicitis and discharge her
